name: CBL syndrome
aliases: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with or without juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia

reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A Noonan-spectrum RASopathy caused by germline variants in CBL, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that normally downregulates receptor tyrosine kinase signalling
Features overlap with Noonan syndrome: short stature, a broad or webbed neck, facial dysmorphism, cryptorchidism and variable developmental delay
The signature association is an increased risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (JMML), sometimes with spontaneous regression after loss of heterozygosity in haematopoietic cells
Some individuals develop a predisposition to vasculitis and other immune or vascular manifestations
The phenotype is highly variable, and carriers may be mildly affected or clinically silent despite the leukaemia predisposition
Recognition matters because it changes cancer surveillance and informs family counselling about JMML risk
Cardiac anomalies, when present, resemble those of the wider RASopathy family and warrant echocardiographic assessment
reference.pathophysiology: CBL encodes a RING-finger E3 ubiquitin ligase and adaptor protein that tags activated receptor tyrosine kinases for degradation, thereby restraining RAS-MAPK signalling. Germline heterozygous variants impair this negative feedback, so the pathway remains inappropriately active, producing the developmental and growth features shared with Noonan syndrome. In haematopoietic progenitors, a second somatic hit that removes the remaining functional allele can drive uncontrolled proliferation and juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia, although the same event may later self-correct, explaining the occasional spontaneous regression.
additionalInvestigations: CBL sequencing within a RASopathy or JMML-predisposition gene panel
Full blood count and blood film with monitoring for monocytosis or cytopenias
Bone marrow examination if haematological abnormality is suspected
Family testing and genetic counselling once a variant is confirmed
redFlags: Persistent monocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly or cytopenias suggesting juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia
Unexplained systemic inflammation or features of vasculitis
Progressive organomegaly or constitutional symptoms in a known carrier
New cardiac symptoms indicating a significant structural lesion
reference.prognosis: Outlook varies widely; many individuals have a mild syndromic phenotype with normal life expectancy, but the risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia is significant, and although some cases regress spontaneously others require intensive haematological treatment.
pitfalls: Overlooking the JMML predisposition because the syndromic features are mild
Assuming any monocytosis is reactive without considering the underlying predisposition
Attributing the phenotype solely to classic Noonan genes and missing CBL
Failing to counsel families about the variable expressivity and cancer risk
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
